name: East Face
approach: Ferry/floatplane to Stehekin (no road access), then the Company Creek Trail roughly 3 miles to a point below Tupshin's west side. Leave the trail and scramble up White Goat Mountain's west slopes through dense brush, traversing rightward through the 4,200-4,600 ft band, then cross a roughly 7,200 ft pass above Bird Lakes and descend into the Bird Lakes basin below Tupshin's east face (face starts ~7,600 ft). Most parties in July to September go in by the Devore Creek trail to the Bird Creek camp near 5,400-5,500 ft, then fight slide alder up to a basin camp around 5,800 ft; easy slopes lead to a ridge near 7,000 ft, then a descending traverse to the snow basin east of the summit block.
descent: Reverse the route: downclimb/rappel the east face's ledge system back to the Bird Lakes basin.
itinerary: Day 1: Ferry/floatplane to Stehekin, hike Company Creek Trail (~3 mi) to the leave-trail point. Day 2: Traverse White Goat Mountain's west slopes and cross the ~7,200 ft pass above Bird Lakes to a high bivy in the Bird Lakes basin. Day 3: Climb the East Face (class 2-4 with a 5.4-5.6 crux) to the summit and return to camp. Day 4: Hike out to Stehekin.

name: Vanishing Point
approach: Start at Barclay Lake trailhead (74920 NE Stevens Pass Hwy, Skykomish, WA 98288). Follow the pleasant level main trail for about 20 minutes to a bridge crossing a large creek (~1 mile). Before the bridge, break right into forest around a large boulder, then walk through relatively open forest or along the creek bed until reaching an open boulder field. Continue through the boulder field to reach steep gullies. Climb around the right side of a chossy waterfall (exposed scrambling). Continue up the wash to a ramp with hand lines, then up a 60–70° forested rib with fixed lines and natural protection, then approximately 800 feet of mostly roped-up slab via bolted sections and natural features. Total approach time: 2.5–3.5 hours for competent parties.
descent: Walk off via the heather descent to a base jumper trail system, then follow well-worn switchbacks through forested ridge system back to the Barclay Lake trailhead parking area. Approximately 3 hours car-to-car from summit.

bivy.name: Dolomite Tower bivy caves
bivy.notes: Shallow caves about 150 ft right of the start of the route. Spray can blow in during wind and rain.
bivy.water: Carry it in or melt from nearby snow early season
bivy.permit: No overnight permit required
bivy.capacity: Three flat platforms, one person each

itinerary: Typically climbed as a 2-3 day trip mirroring the original ascent style: Day 1 — hike in and complete the ~3-3.5 hour technical approach (forested rib with fixed lines, roped slab) to the bivy caves below the tower; Day 2 — climb the full 14-pitch route (a very long day given sustained 5.10-5.12 climbing with few easy pitches); Day 3 (or same-day if fast) — descend via the ~3-hour descent route back to the trailhead. Strong parties also do the route car-to-car in one very long day (roughly 3 hours of approach, a full day on route, and about 3 hours of descent) with a pre-dawn start.

name: Washington Ellinor Traverse (Ridge)
approach: Climb Mount Washington first via its standard south route from the FR 2419 trailhead (see the Standard Route). The traverse itself has no separate trailhead or approach — it begins directly from Washington's summit, heading southwest along the connecting ridge toward Mt. Ellinor rather than descending Washington's standard route.
descent: From Mt. Ellinor's summit, descend via Ellinor's standard trail back to the Ellinor trailhead (a short road walk or car shuttle back to the Washington trailhead on FR 2419).

bivy.name: Big Creek Campground, Lake Cushman
bivy.notes: The obvious roadside base for Mount Ellinor and Mount Washington, sitting at the junction where the Lake Cushman road becomes FR 24, with FR 2419 climbing from there to the Ellinor lower trailhead at about 2,600 ft, the upper trailhead at about 3,500 ft, and the Mount Washington trailhead at the road end near 3,000 ft. Both peaks are genuine day objectives — Ellinor is a maintained trail and Washington a class 3 scramble through a basin and gully — so this is explicitly a contingency rather than the normal plan: it exists for the party that arrives the night before to get an early start on a hot day, or that comes down from the Washington gully later than intended and would rather not drive. It is also the sane base for anyone linking the Washington–Ellinor ridge traverse, which takes far longer than either peak alone. A trail from the campground connects up toward the Mount Ellinor system if you want to walk the whole thing from the tent, but that turns a half-day into a very long one.
bivy.water: Seasonal potable water is generally available in the campground, but do not count on it outside the main summer season. Big Creek runs alongside
bivy.permit: Per-night Forest Service fee. No wilderness permit — this is a developed campground on Forest Service land, outside the national park. Vault toilets, tables and fire rings, pack it in and pack it out. Note the separate parking rule up the hill: a Northwest Forest Pass is required at the Mount Ellinor upper trailhead but not at the lower one, and the Mount Washington trailhead at the end of FR 2419 follows the Forest Service pass regime as well
bivy.capacity: A large forested loop campground — published site counts vary between roughly two dozen and considerably more, so check current numbers rather than trusting a figure. Sites are well spaced in second growth

itinerary: From the Washington trailhead, climb the standard route to Washington's summit (~1.5 hrs at a moderate pace), then traverse the ridge to Ellinor's summit (one GPS-tracked report logged about 4.25 hrs total, trailhead-to-Ellinor-summit, over roughly 6 miles and 4,250 ft of cumulative gain), then descend Ellinor's trail and walk/shuttle back to a car.

name: Waterfall Buttress
approach: From Seattle, drive I-5 north to the Arlington exit, then SR 530 east through Oso to Darrington, and turn onto Squire Creek Road at the west end of town, following it to the parking area where it's gated off by washout damage. From there the approach is long and rough: hike the old roadbed past a landslide crossing (~5 minutes in), reach the original road end around 30-40 minutes from the car, then follow a faint trail through a dry streambed and alder brush, ford Squire Creek, and pick through obscure forest track before finally breaking out into the open basin roughly 2 hours from the car. This is a known bushwhacky, unmaintained approach typical of Darrington-area crags, with route-finding (flagging, cairns) required in several spots.
descent: Rappel the route with 2x60m ropes.

bivy.name: Squire Creek road end / trailhead bivouac
bivy.notes: The Squire Creek road out of the west end of old Darrington has been cut by a washout well short of its historic end for many years, so the drivable road end is A moving target and the walk in to Squire Creek Wall is longer than older descriptions suggest. Parties sleeping in the car or under a tarp at the closure are doing so to get an early start on that extra walking, not because there is anything established there. Confirm the current closure point before committing — how far you can drive has changed repeatedly between seasons, and it is the single biggest variable in a Squire Creek Wall day.
bivy.water: Squire Creek runs close by and is dependable, but needs treating
bivy.permit: None for dispersed camping on forest land; the usual 14-day and setback rules apply.
bivy.capacity: A few parties, informal

bivy.name: Squire Creek Park & Campground, Snohomish County
bivy.notes: Sits in old-growth timber near where Squire Creek meets the North Fork Stillaguamish, a few miles west of Darrington on SR 530 — not on the Mountain Loop Highway, and not up the Squire Creek road itself. It is the most comfortable base for a weekend on the Darrington granite, with flush toilets and a swimmable creek, at the cost of a drive back into town each morning. Because it is county-run rather than Forest Service, the fee schedule, season and reservation window are set separately from the national forest campgrounds and should be checked on their own.
bivy.water: Piped drinking water via spigots through the campground; reliable in season
bivy.permit: None — this is a county park, not Forest Service. Nightly fee, reservations through the Snohomish County Parks system. A Northwest Forest Pass does nothing here.
bivy.capacity: Roughly 30 non-hookup sites, tents and RVs, reservable

itinerary: Feasible as a long single day from the Squire Creek Road trailhead (~3-3.5 hr approach each way plus climbing and rappel descent), or shorten the summit day by hiking in the evening before and bivying at Martha's Place, which sits directly at the base of the buttress approach.

waypoints.name: Squire Creek Park & Campground, Snohomish County

name: Standard Route (South Ridge / South Gully via Copper Glance Basin)
approach: From Winthrop, drive north about 8 miles on West Chewuch Road (County Road 1213) to Eightmile Road (Forest Road 5130), then continue roughly 12-15 miles northwest along Eightmile Creek to the Copper Glance Trailhead (about 3,800-3,810 ft; no fee). Hike Copper Glance Trail #519, which begins on an old mining-claim jeep track/tramway grade (FSR 505) for about 1.5 miles to the historic Copper Glance mine, crosses Copper Glance Creek (the creek's bridge has been reported washed out or missing in some years, requiring a ford), and continues through a 2018 burn area past a small pond to Copper Glance Lake and the open upper basin below Isabella Ridge (about 3.3-3.5 miles one-way, ~6,260-6,600 ft) — a common camp/base for the peak.
descent: Reverse the ascent line: down the south ridge/gully to the basin and out the Copper Glance Trail.

bivy.name: Copper Glance Lake
bivy.notes: This is the only camp that serves Big Craggy and West Craggy, and it belongs to a different drive from everything else in this zone: north from Winthrop on the West Chewuch road, then left onto the Eightmile Creek road and about twelve to thirteen miles to the trailhead at 3,800 feet. Nothing here connects to Harts Pass on foot. The trail climbs steeply for roughly two and a half miles on an old gated mining road past a washed-out bridge and the mine, then becomes a real trail through meadows on the shoulder of Big Craggy to the lake at 6,100 feet. A strong party can car-camp low on the Eightmile Creek road at one of the small Forest Service campgrounds along the creek and take both summits in one long day of about twelve miles and five thousand eight hundred feet, leaving the trail near 5,900 feet for Big Craggy's southeast ridge, then descending to the 7,600 foot saddle and picking a gully onto West Craggy's east ridge. Camping at the lake instead breaks that into something far more pleasant. The upper scree is loose and tiring on the ascent. This is an east-side approach and melts out earlier than the crest, but snow still holds above 5,500 feet well into the early summer, and the Eightmile Creek country has burned repeatedly in recent years so shade and blowdown are both unpredictable.
bivy.water: The lake, and it is reliable. This is the only certain water high on the approach, since the trail above the old mine works is dry through the meadows.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Pasayten permit at the trailhead, no quota. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park at the Copper Glance trailhead. Camp back from the shoreline rather than on it. The lower trail passes old mine workings on patented ground — leave the structures and hardware alone.
bivy.capacity: One good area at the lake taking three or four tents. That is the whole of it, so a busy autumn weekend can fill it and there is no obvious second choice nearby.

itinerary: Day 1: Drive to the Copper Glance Trailhead and hike ~3.3-3.5 miles with ~2,800 ft gain to a camp in Copper Glance Basin (~6,260-6,600 ft). Day 2: From camp, climb ~1,800 ft up talus/scree and the south gully to the south ridge and the summit (roughly 2.5-3 hours one-way), then descend to camp, break camp, and hike out. Strong parties often combine this with Big Craggy Peak and/or do the whole outing car-to-car in one long day.

name: West Face
approach: The standard approach is from the Downey Creek Trailhead (off Suiattle River Road) via the southern end of the Ptarmigan Traverse — a rugged, largely off-trail alpine route over Itswoot Ridge/Cub Lake and Bachelor Creek involving glacier travel and significant bushwhacking. Climbers typically budget a full day (or two) of approach before reaching the base of North Peak's granite West Face; this is an experienced-mountaineers-only objective, not a roadside crag.
descent: From the summit, descend via four double-rope rappels — roughly 50 m, 50 m, 50 m and 20 m — directly from the peak, utilizing existing anchors and natural features on the granite. This brings climbers back to the base of the route. From base camp, descend the approach route in reverse. Some ascents have descended via traversal south to Middle Gunsight and South Gunsight, adding complexity and additional days to the descent.

bivy.name: Dome Glacier and Dome-Chickamin col high bivouacs
bivy.notes: These are the camps that put the eastern peaks in range, and they are the reason parties carry a full glacier kit past Itswoot Ridge. The col between the Dana and Dome glaciers holds a couple of rock rings around 7,470 ft, and further east the Dome-Chickamin col is a genuine high camp with figures around 8,000 ft and above quoted for it. From that eastern col the Chickamin Glacier is the highway to Sinister Peak, whose North Face and Southwest Route are both reached across it, and on to the three Gunsight Range summits beyond, which are granite spires ringed by the Chickamin and Blue glaciers and among the most remote objectives in the state. Parties on the Gunsight peaks routinely cross the Chickamin twice in a day from a camp on this ground. Season is short: the glaciers are best covered from July into August, later brings open crevasses and bare ice, and there is no water, no shelter and no quick way down from any of it.
bivy.water: None running. Every drop is melted snow, and on bare ice years even that takes hunting for. Carry what you can from Cub Lake or the Itswoot Ridge creeks and plan the fuel for melting.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit from the Downey Creek register. Camp on snow, rock or ice. Pack out human waste, which matters more here than anywhere else in the zone because the meltwater below runs straight into the glacier-fed creeks.
bivy.capacity: Rock rings and cleared platforms for one or two parties at a time. At the Dome-Chickamin col there is a flat, large, windy option on the west side and a smaller, harder, calmer one on the east. Nothing else, and no toilet.

bivy.name: Bachelor Creek forest and meadow camps
bivy.notes: This exists because of the brush, and the brush is the single most important thing to understand about the south end. From the Downey Creek trailhead at 1,440 ft the Downey Creek trail runs about six easy forested miles to Sixmile Camp; after that the abandoned Bachelor Creek trail deteriorates badly. The first two miles are tolerable, then it crosses to the south side and turns into slide alder and avalanche deadfall, with reports of sixty or more trees over the trail and long sections where following it is closer to bushwhacking than hiking. Parties routinely take nine to eleven hours from the car to Cub Lake and a slow group with heavy packs can lose the trail entirely. Splitting the approach with a night around the 4,500 ft meadows near the head of the creek is the honest answer for anyone who is not fast, and it is why some parties choose to enter from Cascade Pass and exit here rather than the other way round, so the brush is done downhill and with lighter packs. There is a north-side line through open forest paralleling the creek that some report as better than the trail itself. Everything about this approach is harder than the above suggests: the Suiattle River Road has been closed to vehicles at about milepost 4 after flood damage, under a Forest Service order in effect April 2, 2026 through January 1, 2028 unless rescinded sooner, which leaves roughly sixteen extra road miles each way to a trailhead at mile 20. On top of that, the Forest Service's Miner's Fire order (06-05-26-17) closes the Downey Creek Trailhead, the Downey Creek Trail and the Bachelor Creek Trail from August 15 through December 31, 2026, unless rescinded sooner. The road also spent about a decade closed before reopening in 2014, so a long closure here is the normal state of affairs rather than a surprise. Confirm the road before committing to this end.
bivy.water: Bachelor Creek runs the whole way and is never the problem. The creek crossing itself can be, in high water or early season.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit; Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass on the vehicle at Downey Creek. This is the one part of the zone low enough that a fire is not automatically out of the question, but the ground is wet forest and a stove is the sensible choice.
bivy.capacity: Rough forest sites and a meadow flat near the head of the creek, party-sized only. Nothing established, no toilet.

bivy.name: Cub Lake
bivy.notes: Roughly 12 miles and about 3,900 ft of gain from the Downey Creek trailhead, reached by a steep switchbacking descent off the Bachelor Creek meadows and a walk around the north shore. Parties report anywhere from six hours to eleven getting here, which is a fair measure of how much the brush and the pack weight vary. It is the south-end hub: from the lake the trail climbs to Itswoot Ridge for Spire Point and Dome Peak, and everything on the Chickamin side including Sinister Peak and the Gunsight summits starts from the same ground. Because it is the established camp it also takes the impact, and there is a reasonable argument for camping on the ridge above instead where the ground is less worn, at the cost of carrying water. Coming out, this is where the traverse ends and the brush begins.
bivy.water: The lake, reliable all season. This is the last certain water for anyone heading up onto the ridge and glaciers, and the first on the way out.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit; Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass at the Downey Creek trailhead. Camp 100 feet back from the shore. Practically speaking no fires, and the site is heavily enough used that the surrounding wood is already gone.
bivy.capacity: A well established camp at the lake with room for a few parties, plus meadow sites nearby. It is the most used ground in the southern half of the zone and it shows.

bivy.name: Itswoot Ridge
bivy.notes: This is the working base for the southern peaks and the camp most parties coming in from Downey Creek actually use. Camps are quoted anywhere between roughly 5,900 and 6,400 ft depending on which bench you take, so the number here describes the lower, wetter end of the ridge rather than a single spot. From the benches it is moderate snow of about thirty degrees, or a scree-and-heather line on the left in late season, up to Spire Col at 7,760 ft, and from the col a short descending traverse onto the upper Dana Glacier puts you under the southeast and southwest faces of Spire Point. Dome Peak is the other objective, reached over the Dana Glacier and the Dome Glacier above. Reaching this ridge from the car is a full day with a heavy pack, so plan on arriving late and going nowhere else that evening.
bivy.water: Small running creeks below the lower benches, fed by snowfields on the north side of the ridge, and generally dependable through the normal climbing season. The higher benches toward the col dry out first, so drop back down for water rather than assuming it is there.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit from the Downey Creek trailhead register, plus a Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass on the vehicle. No campfires up here.
bivy.capacity: A string of flat heather benches along the ridge rather than one site, so several parties can spread out without crowding each other. No toilet, no built platforms.

itinerary: Day 1: Hike the Downey Creek Trail and the brushy Bachelor Creek path to camp at Bachelor Flats (about 4,500 ft), or push on to Cub Lake (long day with significant brush and blowdown on Bachelor Creek). Day 2: Over the pass to Cub Lake, up Itswoot Ridge and across the Dome Glacier to a high camp at the Dome-Chickamin col (about 8,500 ft). Day 3: Cross the Chickamin Glacier to the base of the West Face, climb the route (5-6 pitches), rappel, and return to the col. Days 4-5: Hike out over Itswoot Ridge and Cub Lake and down the Bachelor Creek and Downey Creek trails. Carry a spare day for weather.

name: West Ridge
approach: Follow the shared Wine Spires trail: boot path down talus to Early Winters Creek, cross on a log, then climb steeply up the timbered rib north of Burgundy Creek to the ~6,500 ft basin/camp (roughly 2 hours from the car). Paisano Pinnacle's West Ridge route starts lower than Burgundy Spire's and is commonly linked with Burgundy Spire's North Face in one long car-to-car day; fresh water is reported from a spring near the camp bench.
descent: A few hundred feet of downclimbing followed by two rappels (30m, then 20m) into the gully beneath Burgundy Col, downclimbing between anchors, then reverse the approach trail back to the highway.

bivy.name: Bench Camp — larch bench above the Wine Spires pullout
bivy.notes: The one genuinely used high camp on the Kangaroo Ridge side, reached by a steep switchbacking climbers' trail that gains roughly 2,000 ft from the highway. It is the sensible base for Vasiliki Ridge and Vasiliki Tower, for the west side of Juno Tower, and for linking two or three routes over a weekend rather than re-walking the approach each morning. Juno's east-side routes are a different problem — a 2.5 to 3.5 hour approach with a valley camp in Silver Star Creek — and this camp does not serve them. Bugs can be bad in July; water availability is what actually varies.
bivy.water: Present early in the season from snowmelt and the creek drainage, but limited to non-existent by late summer and early autumn. Higher up, a tarn around 7,100 ft and year-round snow at Burgundy Col are the late-season backups.
bivy.permit: None — no reservation, no quota, no backcountry permit. Northwest Forest Pass for the vehicle at the pullout below.
bivy.capacity: Several established tent spots among the larches; the standard base for the north end of the ridge

bivy.name: Lone Fir, Klipchuck and Early Winters campgrounds
bivy.notes: The nearest developed options and the standard choice for a party wanting a table, a toilet and a guaranteed spot rather than a night in a gravel pullout. They descend eastward down the Early Winters Creek valley — Lone Fir around 3,600 ft, Early Winters near 2,200 ft — so they are warmer and considerably lower than the climbing, and Lone Fir is about seven miles from the Blue Lake area. Klipchuck sits back off the highway and is the quietest of the three. All are seasonal and closed when the road is.
bivy.water: Klipchuck and Early Winters have drinking water in season, shut off outside it. Lone Fir has none, but sits on Early Winters Creek, which needs filtering.
bivy.permit: Fee per night, first-come first-served at all three — no reservations, no climbing or backcountry permit. A Northwest Forest Pass is not needed to occupy a site. Fourteen-day stay limit.
bivy.capacity: Roughly 27 sites at Lone Fir, 46 at Klipchuck and about a dozen tent-only sites at Early Winters

itinerary: Commonly climbed car-to-car in a single long day (roughly 10-13 hours total). Many parties instead camp overnight at the ~6,500 ft bench and combine the route with a climb of the Silver Star glacier and/or Burgundy Spire's North Face on the same trip.

name: Windy Peak via Windy Creek Trail (Cathedral Driveway Approach)
approach: From Loomis, drive Toats Coulee Road (FR-39) roughly 22 miles to Long Swamp Campground, then continue about 3 more miles west on FR-39 to the Cathedral Driveway trailhead. The final stretch of road is gravel but reported as smooth/passenger-car friendly. In late June the road from Loomis was mostly paved and the last stretch to the trailhead was broken pavement, slow going, with a small fallen tree that drivers had to lift clear.
descent: Reverse the Windy Creek Trail back to the Cathedral Driveway trailhead.
itinerary: Doable as a single long day given the shorter mileage; can also be paired with a Cathedral Lakes/Cathedral Peak visit from the same general trailhead area for a multi-day trip.

name: Northwest Ridge (Standard Route)
approach: From the Barclay Lake Trailhead (~2,300 ft, reached via Forest Road 6024 off US Highway 2 in Baring), follow Barclay Creek Trail 1055, then leave the maintained trail to bushwhack along Barclay Creek and up Tailgunner Creek to an old, overgrown logging road. A bootpath climbs through forest to about 4,000 ft, crosses a Class 2-3 waterfall ravine, then follows the Tailgunner Couloir (grass and snow patches) to Tailgunner Pass (roughly 5,320-5,360 ft), which lies WNW of the Wing Peak summit. A brushy spur off the forest road about 1,000 ft before the Barclay Lake lot saves roughly 300 ft of walking but is overgrown; parking on the shoulder is easier.
descent: Reverse the northwest ridge back to Tailgunner Pass, with 1-2 short rappels off the summit and upper snow face, then descend the Tailgunner Couloir and the bushwhack approach route back to the Barclay Lake Trailhead.
itinerary: Commonly done as a 2-3 day trip: Day 1, hike/bushwhack from the Barclay Lake Trailhead to camp near Tailgunner Pass (~3,200-3,400 ft gain, roughly 6-7 hrs); Day 2 (optional), tag Gunn Peak and/or Tailgunner Peak from camp; final day, climb Wing Peak's northwest ridge from camp (~2.5 hrs up), then descend all the way to the trailhead (~4 hrs).

name: East Face Variation
approach: From the Alpental/Snow Lake trailhead (~3,100 ft, 1.5 mi north of I-90 Exit 52 via Alpental Rd), hike/skin up the main trail toward Source Lake, then turn south into the valley/basin below The Tooth's east face. In winter, avoid the summer approach path/gully directly below the East Face due to significant avalanche danger; approach via the broader basin instead.
descent: Rappel the South Face route.
itinerary: A single long winter/spring day: early approach from Alpental through the Source Lake basin to the base of the East Face, 5 pitches of mixed/ice/snow climbing, then rappelling the South Face and returning via the same basin approach.

name: Southwest Corner
approach: Same approach as the South Face route to Aasgard Pass (7,841 ft), then hike south toward the tower and ascend snow or Class 2 rock to the col just southwest of the peak (roughly 6-8 hours and about 4,800 ft of gain from the trailhead).
descent: Descend the south face (Class 2-3) back toward the col.
itinerary: Can be done in one day, but parties often recommend two days combined with Dragontail Peak, camping at the col or near Aasgard Pass.

name: West Buttress
approach: Same approach as the other routes: Stuart Lake/Colchuck Lake Trailhead to Colchuck Lake (5,570 ft), then the steep Aasgard Pass trail to the col behind Witches Tower; a steep snowfield crossing (ice axe recommended) leads to the route's base on the west side.
descent: Rappel/downclimb, including an exposed ledge traverse, then descend the snowfield using an ice axe as needed.
itinerary: Documented as a long single day (14 mi round trip, 5,400 ft gain, dawn-to-dark car-to-car) but could be broken into an overnight with a permit and camp near Colchuck Lake or Aasgard Pass.

name: Wright-Pond
approach: From Winthrop, drive west on SR-20 for approximately 28 miles (4.5 miles east of Washington Pass). Turn right on Forest Service Road 400 and follow for 1 mile to the trailhead parking area on the left side of the road.
descent: Rappel the route: 4 double-rope raps on 60m ropes back down the line.

bivy.name: Cutthroat Creek trailhead
bivy.notes: The lot sits a mile up the forest road from SR 20 and has a vault toilet but no water. It is the start for Cutthroat Wall and for the Cutthroat Lake trail toward Cutthroat Pass, and some parties sleep here or in a pullout on the road in before a pre-dawn start, though the lot itself is signed for day use and how strictly that is read varies; dispersed camping in the trees along the forest road below is the uncontroversial option. Access is entirely gated by the SR 20 winter closure, and the road has been shut for construction windows in recent seasons, so confirm before driving out.
bivy.water: None — no potable water at the trailhead. Cutthroat Creek runs below the lot and needs filtering.
bivy.permit: No camping permit and no quota. Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or a day pass covers parking. This is Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, NOT the national park, so there is no backcountry permit system here at all.
bivy.capacity: Large gravel lot, roughly 20-30 vehicles; fills on summer weekends with larch-season hikers

bivy.name: Lone Fir Campground
bivy.notes: The closest developed campground to Washington Pass, on SR 20 along Early Winters Creek six or seven miles east of the pass, just past the turn for the Cutthroat Creek road. Because nothing here can be booked, arriving Friday evening in July or August is a gamble and the fallback is dispersed camping on a spur road. The season runs roughly May or June through September or October, entirely dependent on when the highway opens and when snow returns.
bivy.water: No drinking water at Lone Fir. Early Winters Creek runs through the campground and needs filtering; Klipchuck and Early Winters campgrounds, farther east, have drinking water in season.
bivy.permit: No reservations and no permit — first-come, first-served with a nightly fee. A Northwest Forest Pass is not needed to camp, only to park at the trailhead.
bivy.capacity: 27 sites, tents and small RVs

bivy.name: Klipchuck Campground, with Early Winters nearby
bivy.notes: Klipchuck sits about a quarter mile off SR 20 in fir and pine down-valley toward Mazama, low enough to be warm and dry when the passes are still wet. Early Winters Campground is further east, smaller at around a dozen tent sites, split by the highway near the Methow River, and fills quickly. Both are a longer drive to the trailhead than Lone Fir, which is the tradeoff for a better chance of finding a site on a busy weekend.
bivy.water: Drinking water spigots in season; vault toilets. Water is turned off at the end of the season while the sites stay usable.
bivy.permit: First-come, first-served, nightly fee, no reservation and no permit required.
bivy.capacity: 46 sites, the largest campground on this stretch of highway

bivy.name: Cutthroat Wall base terrace
bivy.notes: The approach leaves the old roadbed a quarter mile from the trailhead at cairns, then climbs left through trees and light brush to a flat bench beneath the west-northwest-facing granite. Most parties do these routes car-to-car in a day, so a bivy here is for a late start or a two-day plan rather than standard practice. The wall faces away from morning sun, which makes an early camp less useful than it looks on the map. The crag is sometimes catalogued under Little Liberty Bell, which is the same approach and the same ground.
bivy.water: No water on the terrace itself. Fill in Cutthroat Creek low on the approach and carry it up.
bivy.permit: None — dispersed national forest camping, no permit and no quota.
bivy.capacity: A small flat area under the cliff; room for one or two parties at most

itinerary: Single-day car-to-car climb: early start, 1-1.5 hr off-trail approach, 4 pitches to III 5.11 (allow several hours given sustained, technical, and runout climbing), 4 raps to descend, reverse the approach.
